tier_reason: First-party wiki table (libvips author) with public driver and per-tool scripts in libvips/vips-bench (vips.c, im.sh, im7.sh, benchmark.sh) and a stated CPU (Threadripper PRO 3955WX), but the measured libraries are Ubuntu 25.04 distribution packages with no compiler version or flags stated; the only compile line is the driver's 'gcc -Wall vips.c `pkg-config vips --cflags --libs`'. Public code plus CPU but missing compiler/flags is C, not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Speed-and-memory-use wiki table (Threadripper PRO 3955WX, Ubuntu 25.04, run 12 Aug 2025): vips-c 8.18 0.57 s, 94.28 MB peak vs ImageMagick convert 7.1.1 4.44 s, 1499.29 MB ('times slower' column 7.79; magick 7.1.1 4.41 s, 7.74). About 16x less peak memory (derived from page data). Single-threaded 1thr-vips-c 0.77 s is about 5.8x faster than convert (derived from page data). Other rows on the same page: GraphicsMagick gm 1.4 2.05 s, pillow-simd 9.5.0 1.51 s, OpenCV 4.10 3.15 s.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the libraries: tools were used 'as packaged for Ubuntu' (Ubuntu 25.04 distribution binaries of libvips 8.18 and ImageMagick 7.1.1). The vips.c driver's comment gives only 'gcc -Wall vips.c `pkg-config vips --cflags --libs` -o vips-c'.
corrections.caveats: Benchmark is first-party (the libvips author's wiki and libvips/vips-bench repo; code public, distro packages, no compiler flags). The page itself says the test 'does a lot of file IO and relatively little processing, which flatters libvips' and that tools which do not thread automatically (Pillow, OpenCV) rank lower than they should on the 16-core machine. Workload is mostly tiled-TIFF I/O plus a bilinear shrink and 3x3 sharpen, so it measures a pipeline rather than a pure resampling kernel. The pipelines are not bit-identical: vips.c runs the 8-bit image through vips_reduce (linear kernel) and an integer-precision convolution, while im.sh/im7.sh use ImageMagick's '-filter triangle -resize 90x90%' and '-convolve' at ImageMagick's default 16-bit quantum depth; outputs are not compared. Times are the quickest real time of five runs with a warm disc cache. The single-thread row (1thr-vips-c 0.77 s) is still about 5.8x faster than convert (derived from page data).

notes: Every number in the record is on the wiki page in the vips-c and convert rows; I only labelled the memory and single-thread ratios as derived and made the compiler field precise. Metadata confirmed on github.com: LGPL-2.1-or-later, 11.7k stars, not archived or forked, last commit 2026-10-02 (active).

tier_reason: RawTherapee issue #6016 (opened 5 Dec 2020 by RawTherapee developer heckflosse) reports 'lab2rgbOut took 5312 ms' without the plugin and 754 ms with it on a 45.6 MP export, but gives no CPU, threads, compiler or flags; the plugin's own PDF has no numbers and its testbed (plugins/fast_float/testbed/fast_float_testbed.c) prints MPixel/sec against stock lcms2 but no results are published. Numbers without methodology are C.

corrections.license: GPL-3.0-or-later for the fast_float plugin (plugins/fast_float source headers say 'version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later version'; COPYING.GPL3 in that directory; the plugin PDF says a paid alternative licence is available from the author). The lcms2 core in the same repo is MIT.
corrections.claimed_speedup: RawTherapee issue #6016: on a 45.6 MP file exported full size to JPEG with the RTv4_sRGB output profile, 'lab2rgbOut took 5312 ms' without the fast-float plugin vs 754 ms with it (about 7x, derived from page data). The plugin PDF ('LittleCMS floating point extensions 1.7') states increased throughput for 8-bit gray/RGB/CMYK transforms and for 32-bit float transforms, without numbers.
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from one RawTherapee developer's comment in an issue (independent of lcms2 but anecdotal): no CPU, thread count, compiler or flags. The plugin is GPL-3.0-or-later (a commercial licence is sold by the author) while the lcms2 core is MIT, so linking it imposes GPL terms on the application. The plugin trades accuracy for speed: its testbed accepts float results that differ from stock lcms2 by up to 0.005 (EPSILON_FLOAT_TESTS) and 0.007 in another check, so the faster path does not reproduce stock lcms2 output exactly. The testbed would let someone reproduce plugin vs no-plugin MPixel/sec, but I found no published results. The baseline is lcms2 itself, not a different library.

notes: Numbers confirmed verbatim on the issue page. Usability changed from mixed to copyable because GPL-3.0-or-later is OSI-approved and no part is unlicensed (precedent: KFR, GPL-2.0-or-later with commercial dual licence, filed copyable); the record's id is the whole lcms2 repo, so check it does not collide with an lcms2-core entry. Metadata on github.com: 751 stars, last commit 2026-10-02 (active); I could not check the 'shipped since lcms2 2.10' claim and left it unchanged.

tier_reason: First-party README ratio ('roughly 3x faster than OpenCV's implementation with AVX2') with a public harness (main.cpp, timing RGB2Y against cv::cvtColor) and a Makefile giving g++ and flags, but no CPU model, no compiler version and no published run output. First-party claim without measured results is C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'Roughly 3x faster than OpenCV's implementation with AVX2, or 2x faster than OpenCV's implementation if using SSE only'; repo description: '2-4x faster than OpenCV'. No measured timings are published. The current RGB2Y.h has only an AVX2 path: the NO_AVX_PLEASE switch the README mentions is not referenced anywhere in the code, so the SSE figure has no code behind it in the current version.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Repo Makefile: g++ -Ofast -std=gnu++17 -fomit-frame-pointer -mavx2 -march=native -mfma -flto -funroll-all-loops -fpeel-loops -ftracer -ftree-vectorize (no compiler version; no published run).
corrections.caveats: Claim is a README ratio with no CPU or measured timings; the harness (main.cpp: 50 warmups, 100 timed runs, both sides multithreaded) is public but its output is not published. Output is not bit-identical to the baseline: RGB2Y rounds each weighted channel term separately (_mm256_mulhrs_epi16 in Q15, then saturating adds), while OpenCV's 8-bit BGR2GRAY rounds the weighted sum once, so some pixels can differ by one grey level; main.cpp checks RGB2Y only against its own scalar reference (RGB2Y_ref, which uses the same per-term rounding), never against cv::cvtColor's output. Each 10-pixel block loads 31 bytes, so the final block of the last row reads at least 1 byte past the end of an unpadded input buffer (main.cpp's synthetic-image path pads by 128 bytes). AVX2 only in the current code; uses the MSVC keyword __forceinline (GCC/Clang portability not checked). The harness uses the OpenCV 3-era CV_BGR2GRAY constant, so it needs changes to build against OpenCV 4, and modern OpenCV may be closer. Code last updated 29 Sep 2018; last commit 23 Mar 2021 only added the MIT LICENSE file.

notes: README and repo description match the record. Metadata on github.com: MIT, 92 stars, 23 forks, not archived or forked, last commit 2021-03-23 (Create LICENSE), so abandoned is correct. The per-term rounding difference from OpenCV and the 1+ byte input over-read are worth carrying into the entry's shortcomings.
